\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2} \sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}}, \end{align} where the last step follows from the two-sided moment estimate for Rademacher sums \cite{montgomerysmith1990rademacher}. Combining \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_scales} and \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_middle_even}, and using \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_covariance_relation}, proves \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness} in the even case.
nodes.statement_short: At even p the Rademacher block yields the larger intermediate scale.

nodes.name: Trace and large-deviation scales
nodes.statement: Now suppose that \(p=2k\) is even. Retaining the first and third terms in \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_lower}, we have \begin{equation} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)^{1/q} \gtrsim_p \frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N} + \|\Lambda\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Keep the first and third terms of (3.21).

nodes.name: Trace and large-deviation scales (3.22)
nodes.statement: \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)^{1/q} \gtrsim_p \frac{\mathrm{Tr}(\Lambda)^{p/2}}{\sqrt N} + \|\Lambda\|^{p/2}\frac{q^{p/2}}{N}.
nodes.label: eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_scales

nodes.name: Test tensor
nodes.statement: It remains to obtain the intermediate fluctuation scale lower bound. Set \[ B:=\frac{\Lambda}{\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}}, \qquad A:=B^{\otimes k}. \] Then \[ \|A\|_{\mathsf F} = \|B\|_{\mathsf F}^k = 1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Introduce B=Lambda/||Lambda||_F and A=B^{otimes k}.

nodes.name: Block test
nodes.statement: Since $\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p}$ is the tensor block of \(S_p\) corresponding entirely to the \(Y\)-coordinates, we have \begin{equation} \|S_p\|_{\mathsf F} \ge \bigg\| \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p} \bigg\|_{\mathsf F} \ge \bigg| \bigg\langle A, \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p} \bigg\rangle_{\mathsf F} \bigg|. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to the Y-block and test against A.

nodes.name: Rademacher-block test (3.23)
nodes.statement: \|S_p\|_{\mathsf F} \ge \bigg\| \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p} \bigg\|_{\mathsf F} \ge \bigg| \bigg\langle A, \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p} \bigg\rangle_{\mathsf F} \bigg|.
nodes.label: eq:subgaussian_tensor_block_test

nodes.name: Contraction is a power of R
nodes.statement: Since \(Y=R\Lambda^{1/2}\varepsilon\) and every coordinate of \(\varepsilon\) takes values in \(\{\pm 1\}\), \[ Y^\top B Y = \frac{R^2}{\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}} \varepsilon^\top\Lambda^2\varepsilon = \frac{R^2}{\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}} \sum_{j=1}^d\lambda_j^2 = R^2\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}. \] Consequently, recalling that \(p=2k\), \[ \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\langle A,Y^{\otimes p}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rangle_{\mathsf F} = \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\langle B^{\otimes k},Y^{\otimes 2k}\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rangle_{\mathsf F} = (Y^\top B Y)^k = R^{2k}\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^k. \]
nodes.statement_short: The contraction equals R^{2k}||Lambda||_F^k.

nodes.name: Rademacher reduction
nodes.statement: For \( i = 1, \ldots, N\), define the Rademacher random variable \(\eta_i\) by \[ R_i^{2k}-\mathbb{E} R^{2k} = 2^{k-1}\eta_i. \] Then \(\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_N\) are independent, and \[ \bigg\langle A, \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N Y_i^{\otimes p}-\mathbb{E} Y^{\otimes p} \bigg\rangle_{\mathsf F} = 2^{k-1}\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^k \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\eta_i. \]
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the centered contraction as a Rademacher average.

nodes.name: Rademacher moments
nodes.statement: Combining this identity with \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_block_test} and taking \(L_q\)-norms, we obtain \begin{align} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)^{1/q} \ge 2^{k-1}\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^k \bigg\| \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\eta_i \bigg\|_{L_q} \asymp_p \|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2} \sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}}, \end{align} where the last step follows from the two-sided moment estimate for Rademacher sums \cite{montgomerysmith1990rademacher}.
nodes.statement_short: Two-sided Rademacher moment estimate gives ||Lambda||_F^{p/2}sqrt((q^N)/N).

nodes.name: Intermediate even-order lower bound (3.24)
nodes.statement: \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left(\mathbb{E}\|S_p\|_{\mathsf F}^q\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right)^{1/q} \ge 2^{k-1}\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^k \bigg\| \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\eta_i \bigg\|_{L_q} \asymp_p \|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{p/2} \sqrt{\frac{q\land N}{N}},
nodes.label: eq:subgaussian_tensor_middle_even

nodes.name: Conclude the even case
nodes.statement: Combining \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_gaussian_scales} and \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_middle_even}, and using \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_covariance_relation}, proves \eqref{eq:subgaussian_tensor_sharpness} in the even case.
nodes.statement_short: Combine the scales.

nodes.name: Why the sub-Gaussian and Gaussian bounds differ
nodes.statement: The distinction is already visible at order \(p=2\). At this order, the intermediate covariance scale is determined by the largest \(L_2\)-fluctuation of a centered quadratic form. Since \(G^{\otimes2}-\Lambda\) is symmetric, it suffices to consider symmetric matrices \(A\). The Gaussian fourth-moment identity gives \[ \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\langle A,G^{\otimes2}-\Lambda \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rangle_{\mathsf F}^{2} = 2\|\Lambda^{1/2}A\Lambda^{1/2}\|_{\mathsf F}^{2} \le 2\|\Lambda\|^2\|A\|_{\mathsf F}^2. \] Taking \(A\) to be the orthogonal projector onto a top eigendirection of \(\Lambda\) gives equality. Therefore, \[ \sup_{\|A\|_{\mathsf F}\le1} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\langle A,G^{\otimes2}-\Lambda \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rangle_{\mathsf F} \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{L_2} = \sqrt2\,\|\Lambda\|. \] Condition~\eqref{eq:def-subg} controls linear functionals, but places no comparable restriction on the dependence among quadratic fluctuations. For the random-radius block \(Y\) above, take \(B=\Lambda/\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}\). Then \[ \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\langle B,Y^{\otimes2}-\Lambda \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rangle_{\mathsf F} = (R^2-1)\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}, \] whose \(L_2\)-norm is \(\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}\). Thus \(G\) and \(Y\) have the same covariance and both satisfy \eqref{eq:def-subg} with constants of order one, but their quadratic fluctuations can occur on different scales. Indeed, in the eigenbasis of \(\Lambda\), \(Y_j^2-\mathbb{E} Y_j^2=(R^2-1)\lambda_j\) for every \(j\). The same random factor therefore makes the energy fluctuations in all eigendirections have the same sign, so they add without cancellation. The sub-Gaussian control of linear projections does not rule out this dependence. For \(G\), by contrast, the coordinate energies are independent, and the fourth-moment identity yields the spectral scale \(\|\Lambda\|\). For higher orders, the same distinction appears through the Gaussian chaos decomposition and the contractions used above. When \(p=2k\), centering removes the zeroth Gaussian chaos, which is the sum of all complete Wick pairings. The lowest nonzero chaos has order two and is formed from \(k-1\) covariance factors and one centered quadratic Gaussian factor. Its largest \(L_2\)-fluctuation has, up to constants depending only on \(p\), the scale \(\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{k-1}\|\Lambda\|\), and the higher Gaussian chaoses are no larger. For the random-radius construction, by contrast, the contraction against \(B^{\otimes k}\) remains random after centering and has scale \(\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{k}\). When \(p=2k+1\), a complete pairing is impossible. The lowest Gaussian chaos has order one, while the analogous contraction for the random-radius block also retains one linear factor. The largest \(L_2\)-scale of this factor is \(\|\Lambda\|^{1/2}\), giving \(\|\Lambda\|_{\mathsf F}^{k}\|\Lambda\|^{1/2}\) in both cases. Thus the quadratic-fluctuation gap visible at order two persists at even orders, whereas at odd orders the unavoidable linear factor gives the same covariance scale.
nodes.statement_short: Sub-Gaussianity controls linear marginals but not dependence of quadratic fluctuations: a common random radius aligns energy fluctuations, giving scale ||Lambda||_F^k at even orders.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement:
\medskip 
oindent	extbf{Step 1: Reduction to finite support and strict slack.} \medskip Set $E:=\operatorname{Ran}(\Sigma)$. For every \(v\in\ker(\Sigma)\), convex domination applied to \(x\mapsto|\langle v,xangle|\) gives \[ \mathbb{E}|\langle v,Zangle| \le \mathbb{E}|\langle v,G_\Sigmaangle| = 0. \] Thus \(Z\in E\) almost surely. Restricting \(\Sigma\) and every input leg of \(T\) to \(E\) does not change \(T(Z,\ldots,Z)\) or \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\), and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\). Moreover, since $E=\ker(\Sigma)^\perp$, the restriction of \(\Sigma\) to \(E\) is positive definite. After identifying \(E\) with \(\mathbb R^{\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)}\), we may therefore assume that \(\Sigma\) is positive definite. Let \(G\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). Since convex order is preserved under linear maps, $\Sigma^{-1/2}Z \preceq_{\mathrm{cx}} G$. Applying \cite[Lemma~3.1]{hua2026talagrand} to \(\Sigma^{-1/2}Z\), we obtain centered finitely supported random vectors \(Y_n\) such that $Y_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}G$ and \(Y_n\) converges in distribution to \(\Sigma^{-1/2}Z\). Define $Z_n:=\Sigma^{1/2}Y_n.$ It follows that \[ Z_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}G_\Sigma \qquad	ext{and}\qquad Z_n\Longrightarrow Z. \] Choose \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\) with \(0<\varepsilon_n<1\), and set \(\widetilde Z_n:=(1-\varepsilon_n)Z_n\). Since convex order is preserved under linear maps, \[ \widetilde Z_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon_n)G_\Sigma \qquad	ext{and}\qquad \widetilde Z_n\Longrightarrow Z. \] It therefore suffices to prove the estimate, with a constant \(C_p\) depending only on \(p\) and in particular independent of \(\varepsilon\) and of the distribution of \(W\), for every centered finitely supported random vector \(W\) satisfying \(W\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon)G_\Sigma\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Indeed, applying this estimate to \(W=\widetilde Z_n\), and using that \(x\mapsto T(x,\ldots,x)\) is continuous together with the lower semicontinuity of nonnegative moments under convergence in distribution, we obtain \[ \mathbb{E} ig\|T(Z,\ldots,Z) ig\|_{\mathcal H}^q \le \liminf_{n	o\infty} \mathbb{E} ig\|T(\widetilde Z_n,\ldots,\widetilde Z_n) ig\|_{\mathcal H}^q \le C_p^q\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)^q\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^q. \] Consequently, it suffices to prove the result when  egin{equation} Z 	ext{ has finite support}, \qquad Z\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon)G_\Sigma 	ext{ for some } \varepsilon\in(0,1). \end{equation} \medskip 
oindent	extbf{Step 2: Structured martingale coupling and conditional moments.} \medskip We now work under the additional assumption \eqref{eq:Lq-strict-slack}. Write \[ \mathrm{supp}(Z)=\{z_1,\ldots,z_s\}, \qquad \mathbb P(Z=z_i)=w_i>0. \] By the strict-slack part of \cite[Proposition~3.3]{hua2026talagrand}, \(Z\) and \(G_\Sigma\) admit a martingale coupling whose conditional densities are exponential tilts: the law of \(G_\Sigma\) given \(Z=z_i\) has density \(f_i\) with respect to \(\gamma_\Sigma:=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)\) given by \[ f_i(y):=  rac{\exp igl(a_i+\langle b_i,yangle igr)}{D(y)}, \qquad D(y):= \sum_{j=1}^s w_j\exp igl(a_j+\langle b_j,yangle igr), \] for suitable \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\in\mathbb R\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\in\mathbb R^d\). Moreover,  egin{align} \int_{\mathbb R^d}f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=1, \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}y f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=z_i, \end{align} the second identity expressing the martingale property \(\mathbb{E}[G_\Sigma\mid Z]=Z\). Set \[ R:=G_\Sigma-Z, \qquad M_r(z_i):=\mathbb{E}[R^{\otimes r}\mid Z=z_i],\ \ r\ge 1. \] In particular, the second identity in \eqref{eq:theorem2_proof_aux1} gives \(M_1(z_i)=0\). Conditionally on \(Z=z_i\), the random vector \(R\) has density proportional to \[ y\longmapsto \exp igl(-\mathcal V_i(y) igr), \] where \[ \mathcal V_i(y) :=  rac12 \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left\langle y+z_i,\Sigma^{-1}(y+z_i) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupightangle -\log f_i(y+z_i). \] Since \(f_i\) is a strictly positive finite softmax function, \(\mathcal V_i\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\). Furthermore, defining \[ \alpha_j(y) :=  rac{ w_j\exp igl(a_j+\langle b_j,yangle igr) }{ D(y) }, \qquad \overline b(y):= \sum_{j=1}^s\alpha_j(y)b_j, \] we have  egin{align*} 
abla^2\mathcal V_i(y) &= \Sigma^{-1} + 
abla^2\log D(y+z_i)\ &= \Sigma^{-1} + \sum_{j=1}^s \alpha_j(y+z_i)  igl(b_j-\overline b(y+z_i) igr)  igl(b_j-\overline b(y+z_i) igr)^	op\ &\succeq \Sigma^{-1}. \end{align*} Thus the conditional law of \(R\) given \(Z=z_i\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition~ef{prop:ULC-moment-tensors}, which gives  egin{equation} \|M_r(z_i)\|_{\mathsf F} \le U_rho_r(\Sigma), \qquad 1\le i\le s, \end{equation} where \(U_r\) is a constant depending only on \(r\), and \(ho_r(\Sigma)\) is as in the proposition. \medskip 
oindent	extbf{Step 3: Conditional expansion and the Gaussian term.} \medskip In what follows, let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) denote the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(0\le r\le p\) and \(B\in(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}\), write \[ B = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d B_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}, \] and define \[ T[Z^{p-r},B] := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d B_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} T( \underbrace{Z,\ldots,Z}_{p-r	ext{ times}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ). \] When \(r=p\), the \(Z\)-arguments are omitted; when $r=0$, $T[Z^p] = T(Z,\ldots,Z)$. Since symmetrizing \(T\) does not change \(T(Z,\ldots,Z)\) and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\) is symmetric. We prove the desired estimate simultaneously for all \(q\ge1\) and all finite-dimensional target Hilbert spaces by induction on \(p\). For \(p=1\), the function \[ x\longmapsto\|T(x)\|_{\mathcal H}^q \] is convex. Hence the assumed convex domination and Proposition~ef{prop:Hilbert-Gaussian-tensor-Lq} give \[ \|T(Z)\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \|T(G_\Sigma)\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \lesssim \Psi_1(q,\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \] Let \(p\ge2\), and suppose that the assertion has been proved through degree \(p-1\). Expanding \(T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)=T(Z+R,\ldots,Z+R)\) by multilinearity produces, for each \(0\le r\le p\), the \( inom pr\) terms in which \(r\) arguments equal \(R\) and the remaining \(p-r\) equal \(Z\). Since \(T\) is symmetric, all terms with the same \(r\) coincide, and therefore \[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{r=0}^p  inom pr T[Z^{p-r},R^{\otimes r}]. \] Taking conditional expectation given \(Z\), we obtain  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ T[Z^{p-r},R^{\otimes r}] \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight] = T\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ Z^{p-r}, \mathbb{E}[R^{\otimes r}\mid Z] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight]= T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align*} The term corresponding to \(r=0\) is \(T[Z^p]\), while the term corresponding to \(r=1\) vanishes because $M_1(Z) = \mathbb{E}[R\mid Z] = 0$. Consequently,  egin{align*} \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight] = T[Z^p] + \sum_{r=2}^p  inom pr T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align*} Rearranging this identity, we obtain  egin{align} T[Z^p] = \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight] - \sum_{r=2}^p  inom pr T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align} We next control $\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight]$. Since \(y\mapsto\|y\|_{\mathcal H}^q\) is convex for \(q\ge1\), conditional Jensen's inequality gives  egin{align*} \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left\| \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight\|_{\mathcal H}^q\le \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[  ig\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)  ig\|_{\mathcal H}^q \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight]= \mathbb{E}  ig\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)  ig\|_{\mathcal H}^q. \end{align*} Taking \(q\)-th roots and applying Proposition~ef{prop:Hilbert-Gaussian-tensor-Lq} yield  egin{align} \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left\| \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le g_p \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}, \end{align} where \(g_p\) depends only on \(p\). \medskip 
oindent	extbf{Step 4: Lower-order terms and completion of the induction.} \medskip For \(2\le r\le p-1\), we equip $\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}$ with its natural Hilbert-space structure. More precisely, if \[ U = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} \otimes e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}, \qquad h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\in\mathcal H, \] then \[ \|U\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}^2 := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d \|h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\|_{\mathcal H}^2. \] Define the \((p-r)\)-linear map \[ \mathcal S_rT: (\mathbb R^d)^{p-r} \longrightarrow \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} \] by  egin{align*} (\mathcal S_rT)(x_1,\ldots,x_{p-r}) := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d T(x_1,\ldots,x_{p-r},e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r})\otimes e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}. \end{align*} By the definition of the Frobenius norm of a multilinear map,  egin{align*} \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F}^2 &= \sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_{p-r}=1}^d  ig\| (\mathcal S_rT) (e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_{p-r}})  ig\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}^2\ &= \sum_{\substack{ j_1,\ldots,j_{p-r}=1\ i_1,\ldots,i_r=1 }}^d  ig\| T( e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_{p-r}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} )  ig\|_{\mathcal H}^2= \|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2. \end{align*} Therefore, \[ \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F} = \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \] We next relate \(\mathcal S_rT\) to the contraction appearing in \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-expansion}. By definition,  egin{align*} T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\, T( \underbrace{Z,\ldots,Z}_{p-r	ext{ times}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ). \end{align*} Hence, by the triangle inequality followed by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality,  egin{align*}  ig\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]  ig\|_{\mathcal H} &\le \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d  ig| (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}  ig|	imes  ig\| T( Z,\ldots,Z, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} )  ig\|_{\mathcal H}\ &\le  igg( \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}^2  igg)^{1/2}  igg( \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d  ig\| T( Z,\ldots,Z, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} )  ig\|_{\mathcal H}^2  igg)^{1/2}\ &= \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F}  ig\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z)  ig\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}. \end{align*} Thus, pointwise, \[  ig\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]  ig\|_{\mathcal H} \le  ig\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z)  ig\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}} \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F}. \] By \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Mr}, \[ \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F} \le U_rho_r(\Sigma) \] almost surely. Therefore, taking \(L_q\)-norms in the preceding pointwise inequality gives  egin{align}  ig\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]  ig\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rho_r(\Sigma)  ig\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z)  ig\|_{L_q( \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} )}. \end{align} Let \(Q_k\) denote the constant in the induction hypothesis at degree \(k\). More precisely, the induction hypothesis states that, for every finite-dimensional Hilbert space \(\mathcal K\) and every \(k\)-linear map \[ S:(\mathbb R^d)^k	o\mathcal K, \] one has \[  ig\| S(Z,\ldots,Z)  ig\|_{L_q(\mathcal K)} \le Q_k \Psi_k(q,\Sigma) \|S\|_{\mathsf F}. \] The space $\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}$ is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and \(\mathcal S_rT\) is an \((p-r)\)-linear map taking values in this space. We may therefore apply the induction hypothesis at degree \(p-r\) to \(\mathcal S_rT\). This gives  egin{align*}  ig\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z)  ig\|_{L_q( \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} )} \le Q_{p-r} \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F}= Q_{p-r} \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Substituting this estimate into \eqref{eq:Lq-correction-first-bound}, we obtain  egin{align}  ig\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]  ig\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rQ_{p-r} ho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align} It remains to compare the two covariance scales. We claim that  egin{equation} ho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \qquad 2\le r\le p-1. \end{equation} Suppose first that \(r\) is even. Then $ho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2}$, and hence  egin{align*} ho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-r-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\ &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\ j\equiv p\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma). \end{align*} Now suppose that \(r\) is odd. Then $ho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(r-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{1/2}$, and  egin{align*} ho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{j/2}\ &\le \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{(j+1)/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \end{align*} where the first inequality uses \(q\ge1\). For every index \(j\) in the last sum, \(j+1\equiv p\pmod 2\), so its summand is one of the summands defining \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\). This proves \eqref{eq:rho-Psi-product}. Combining \eqref{eq:Lq-correction-before-scales} and \eqref{eq:rho-Psi-product}, we conclude that \[  ig\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]  ig\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rQ_{p-r} \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}, \qquad 2\le r\le p-1. \] The term corresponding to \(r=p\) is estimated directly. By \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Mr},  egin{align*}  ig\| T[M_p(Z)]  ig\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \|T\|_{\mathsf F}  ig\| \|M_p(Z)\|_{\mathsf F}  ig\|_{L_q}\le U_pho_p(\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\le U_p\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Using the representation of \(T[Z^p]\) in \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-expansion}, and combining the preceding estimates with \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Gaussian}, gives  egin{align*} \|T[Z^p]\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le  igg( g_p + U_p + \sum_{r=2}^{p-1}  inom pr U_rQ_{p-r}  igg) \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Thus the induction closes with $Q_1:=g_1$ and, for \(p\ge2\), \[ Q_p := g_p + U_p + \sum_{r=2}^{p-1}  inom pr U_rQ_{p-r}, \] where the sum is understood to be empty when \(p=2\). In particular, \(Q_p\) depends only on \(p\) and is independent of \(q\), the dimension $d$, \(\Sigma\), the support of \(Z\), and the strict-slack parameter \(\varepsilon\). This proves the desired estimate in the finite-support strict-slack case. The approximation argument in 	extbf{Step~1} completes the proof in full generality.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to finitely supported Z with strict slack, use the Hua-Song-Tudose coupling with uniformly log-concave remainders, expand conditionally, and close the induction on p. Key step: rho_r Psi_{p-r} <= Psi_p.

nodes.name: Step 1: reduction to finite support and strict slack
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 1: Reduction to finite support and strict slack.} \medskip Set $E:=\operatorname{Ran}(\Sigma)$. For every \(v\in\ker(\Sigma)\), convex domination applied to \(x\mapsto|\langle v,x\rangle|\) gives \[ \mathbb{E}|\langle v,Z\rangle| \le \mathbb{E}|\langle v,G_\Sigma\rangle| = 0. \] Thus \(Z\in E\) almost surely. Restricting \(\Sigma\) and every input leg of \(T\) to \(E\) does not change \(T(Z,\ldots,Z)\) or \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\), and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\). Moreover, since $E=\ker(\Sigma)^\perp$, the restriction of \(\Sigma\) to \(E\) is positive definite. After identifying \(E\) with \(\mathbb R^{\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)}\), we may therefore assume that \(\Sigma\) is positive definite. Let \(G\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). Since convex order is preserved under linear maps, $\Sigma^{-1/2}Z \preceq_{\mathrm{cx}} G$. Applying \cite[Lemma~3.1]{hua2026talagrand} to \(\Sigma^{-1/2}Z\), we obtain centered finitely supported random vectors \(Y_n\) such that $Y_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}G$ and \(Y_n\) converges in distribution to \(\Sigma^{-1/2}Z\). Define $Z_n:=\Sigma^{1/2}Y_n.$ It follows that \[ Z_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}G_\Sigma \qquad\text{and}\qquad Z_n\Longrightarrow Z. \] Choose \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\) with \(0<\varepsilon_n<1\), and set \(\widetilde Z_n:=(1-\varepsilon_n)Z_n\). Since convex order is preserved under linear maps, \[ \widetilde Z_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon_n)G_\Sigma \qquad\text{and}\qquad \widetilde Z_n\Longrightarrow Z. \] It therefore suffices to prove the estimate, with a constant \(C_p\) depending only on \(p\) and in particular independent of \(\varepsilon\) and of the distribution of \(W\), for every centered finitely supported random vector \(W\) satisfying \(W\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon)G_\Sigma\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Indeed, applying this estimate to \(W=\widetilde Z_n\), and using that \(x\mapsto T(x,\ldots,x)\) is continuous together with the lower semicontinuity of nonnegative moments under convergence in distribution, we obtain \[ \mathbb{E}\big\|T(Z,\ldots,Z)\big\|_{\mathcal H}^q \le \liminf_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\big\|T(\widetilde Z_n,\ldots,\widetilde Z_n)\big\|_{\mathcal H}^q \le C_p^q\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)^q\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^q. \] Consequently, it suffices to prove the result when \begin{equation} Z \text{ has finite support}, \qquad Z\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon)G_\Sigma \text{ for some } \varepsilon\in(0,1). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to positive definite Sigma and finitely supported Z with strict slack.

nodes.name: Restrict to the range of Sigma
nodes.statement: Set $E:=\operatorname{Ran}(\Sigma)$. For every \(v\in\ker(\Sigma)\), convex domination applied to \(x\mapsto|\langle v,x\rangle|\) gives \[ \mathbb{E}|\langle v,Z\rangle| \le \mathbb{E}|\langle v,G_\Sigma\rangle| = 0. \] Thus \(Z\in E\) almost surely. Restricting \(\Sigma\) and every input leg of \(T\) to \(E\) does not change \(T(Z,\ldots,Z)\) or \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\), and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\). Moreover, since $E=\ker(\Sigma)^\perp$, the restriction of \(\Sigma\) to \(E\) is positive definite. After identifying \(E\) with \(\mathbb R^{\operatorname{rank}(\Sigma)}\), we may therefore assume that \(\Sigma\) is positive definite.
nodes.statement_short: Z lives in Ran(Sigma), so assume Sigma positive definite.

nodes.name: Finite-support approximation
nodes.statement: Let \(G\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). Since convex order is preserved under linear maps, $\Sigma^{-1/2}Z \preceq_{\mathrm{cx}} G$. Applying \cite[Lemma~3.1]{hua2026talagrand} to \(\Sigma^{-1/2}Z\), we obtain centered finitely supported random vectors \(Y_n\) such that $Y_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}G$ and \(Y_n\) converges in distribution to \(\Sigma^{-1/2}Z\). Define $Z_n:=\Sigma^{1/2}Y_n.$ It follows that \[ Z_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}G_\Sigma \qquad\text{and}\qquad Z_n\Longrightarrow Z. \]
nodes.statement_short: Hua-Song-Tudose Lemma 3.1 gives finitely supported approximants Z_n.

nodes.name: Introduce strict slack
nodes.statement: Choose \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\) with \(0<\varepsilon_n<1\), and set \(\widetilde Z_n:=(1-\varepsilon_n)Z_n\). Since convex order is preserved under linear maps, \[ \widetilde Z_n\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon_n)G_\Sigma \qquad\text{and}\qquad \widetilde Z_n\Longrightarrow Z. \]
nodes.statement_short: Shrink Z_n by (1-eps_n).

nodes.name: Reduction by lower semicontinuity
nodes.statement: It therefore suffices to prove the estimate, with a constant \(C_p\) depending only on \(p\) and in particular independent of \(\varepsilon\) and of the distribution of \(W\), for every centered finitely supported random vector \(W\) satisfying \(W\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon)G_\Sigma\) with \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Indeed, applying this estimate to \(W=\widetilde Z_n\), and using that \(x\mapsto T(x,\ldots,x)\) is continuous together with the lower semicontinuity of nonnegative moments under convergence in distribution, we obtain \[ \mathbb{E}\big\|T(Z,\ldots,Z)\big\|_{\mathcal H}^q \le \liminf_{n\to\infty} \mathbb{E}\big\|T(\widetilde Z_n,\ldots,\widetilde Z_n)\big\|_{\mathcal H}^q \le C_p^q\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)^q\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^q. \] Consequently, it suffices to prove the result when \begin{equation} Z \text{ has finite support}, \qquad Z\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon)G_\Sigma \text{ for some } \varepsilon\in(0,1). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Lower semicontinuity of moments transfers the bound to Z.

nodes.name: Finite support and strict slack (4.1)
nodes.statement: Z \text{ has finite support}, \qquad Z\preceq_{\mathrm{cx}}(1-\varepsilon)G_\Sigma \text{ for some } \varepsilon\in(0,1).
nodes.label: eq:Lq-strict-slack

nodes.name: Step 2: structured martingale coupling and conditional moments
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 2: Structured martingale coupling and conditional moments.} \medskip We now work under the additional assumption \eqref{eq:Lq-strict-slack}. Write \[ \mathrm{supp}(Z)=\{z_1,\ldots,z_s\}, \qquad \mathbb P(Z=z_i)=w_i>0. \] By the strict-slack part of \cite[Proposition~3.3]{hua2026talagrand}, \(Z\) and \(G_\Sigma\) admit a martingale coupling whose conditional densities are exponential tilts: the law of \(G_\Sigma\) given \(Z=z_i\) has density \(f_i\) with respect to \(\gamma_\Sigma:=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)\) given by \[ f_i(y):= \frac{\exp\bigl(a_i+\langle b_i,y\rangle\bigr)}{D(y)}, \qquad D(y):= \sum_{j=1}^s w_j\exp\bigl(a_j+\langle b_j,y\rangle\bigr), \] for suitable \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\in\mathbb R\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\in\mathbb R^d\). Moreover, \begin{align} \int_{\mathbb R^d}f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=1, \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}y f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=z_i, \end{align} the second identity expressing the martingale property \(\mathbb{E}[G_\Sigma\mid Z]=Z\). Set \[ R:=G_\Sigma-Z, \qquad M_r(z_i):=\mathbb{E}[R^{\otimes r}\mid Z=z_i],\ \ r\ge 1. \] In particular, the second identity in \eqref{eq:theorem2_proof_aux1} gives \(M_1(z_i)=0\). Conditionally on \(Z=z_i\), the random vector \(R\) has density proportional to \[ y\longmapsto \exp\bigl(-\mathcal V_i(y)\bigr), \] where \[ \mathcal V_i(y) := \frac12 \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\langle y+z_i,\Sigma^{-1}(y+z_i) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rangle -\log f_i(y+z_i). \] Since \(f_i\) is a strictly positive finite softmax function, \(\mathcal V_i\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\). Furthermore, defining \[ \alpha_j(y) := \frac{ w_j\exp\bigl(a_j+\langle b_j,y\rangle\bigr) }{ D(y) }, \qquad \overline b(y):= \sum_{j=1}^s\alpha_j(y)b_j, \] we have \begin{align*} \nabla^2\mathcal V_i(y) &= \Sigma^{-1} + \nabla^2\log D(y+z_i)\\ &= \Sigma^{-1} + \sum_{j=1}^s \alpha_j(y+z_i) \bigl(b_j-\overline b(y+z_i)\bigr) \bigl(b_j-\overline b(y+z_i)\bigr)^\top\\ &\succeq \Sigma^{-1}. \end{align*} Thus the conditional law of \(R\) given \(Z=z_i\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition~\ref{prop:ULC-moment-tensors}, which gives \begin{equation} \|M_r(z_i)\|_{\mathsf F} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma), \qquad 1\le i\le s, \end{equation} where \(U_r\) is a constant depending only on \(r\), and \(\rho_r(\Sigma)\) is as in the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: The coupling has uniformly log-concave conditional remainders, so Proposition 2.4 bounds M_r.

nodes.name: Finite support notation
nodes.statement: We now work under the additional assumption \eqref{eq:Lq-strict-slack}. Write \[ \mathrm{supp}(Z)=\{z_1,\ldots,z_s\}, \qquad \mathbb P(Z=z_i)=w_i>0. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write the support and weights of Z.

nodes.name: Exponential-tilt coupling
nodes.statement: By the strict-slack part of \cite[Proposition~3.3]{hua2026talagrand}, \(Z\) and \(G_\Sigma\) admit a martingale coupling whose conditional densities are exponential tilts: the law of \(G_\Sigma\) given \(Z=z_i\) has density \(f_i\) with respect to \(\gamma_\Sigma:=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)\) given by \[ f_i(y):= \frac{\exp\bigl(a_i+\langle b_i,y\rangle\bigr)}{D(y)}, \qquad D(y):= \sum_{j=1}^s w_j\exp\bigl(a_j+\langle b_j,y\rangle\bigr), \] for suitable \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\in\mathbb R\) and \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\in\mathbb R^d\). Moreover, \begin{align} \int_{\mathbb R^d}f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=1, \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}y f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=z_i, \end{align} the second identity expressing the martingale property \(\mathbb{E}[G_\Sigma\mid Z]=Z\). Set \[ R:=G_\Sigma-Z, \qquad M_r(z_i):=\mathbb{E}[R^{\otimes r}\mid Z=z_i],\ \ r\ge 1. \] In particular, the second identity in \eqref{eq:theorem2_proof_aux1} gives \(M_1(z_i)=0\).
nodes.statement_short: Hua-Song-Tudose Proposition 3.3 gives a martingale coupling with exponential-tilt densities.

nodes.name: Martingale coupling identities (4.2)
nodes.statement: \int_{\mathbb R^d}f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=1, \qquad \int_{\mathbb R^d}y f_i(y)\,\gamma_\Sigma(dy)=z_i,
nodes.label: eq:theorem2_proof_aux1

nodes.name: Hessian lower bound
nodes.statement: Conditionally on \(Z=z_i\), the random vector \(R\) has density proportional to \[ y\longmapsto \exp\bigl(-\mathcal V_i(y)\bigr), \] where \[ \mathcal V_i(y) := \frac12 \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\langle y+z_i,\Sigma^{-1}(y+z_i) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\rangle -\log f_i(y+z_i). \] Since \(f_i\) is a strictly positive finite softmax function, \(\mathcal V_i\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)\). Furthermore, defining \[ \alpha_j(y) := \frac{ w_j\exp\bigl(a_j+\langle b_j,y\rangle\bigr) }{ D(y) }, \qquad \overline b(y):= \sum_{j=1}^s\alpha_j(y)b_j, \] we have \begin{align*} \nabla^2\mathcal V_i(y) &= \Sigma^{-1} + \nabla^2\log D(y+z_i)\\ &= \Sigma^{-1} + \sum_{j=1}^s \alpha_j(y+z_i) \bigl(b_j-\overline b(y+z_i)\bigr) \bigl(b_j-\overline b(y+z_i)\bigr)^\top\\ &\succeq \Sigma^{-1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The conditional potential has Hessian at least Sigma^{-1}.

nodes.name: Bound conditional moment tensors
nodes.statement: Thus the conditional law of \(R\) given \(Z=z_i\) satisfies the assumptions of Proposition~\ref{prop:ULC-moment-tensors}, which gives \begin{equation} \|M_r(z_i)\|_{\mathsf F} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma), \qquad 1\le i\le s, \end{equation} where \(U_r\) is a constant depending only on \(r\), and \(\rho_r(\Sigma)\) is as in the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.4 gives ||M_r(z_i)||_F <= U_r rho_r(Sigma).

nodes.name: Conditional moment tensor bound (4.3)
nodes.statement: \|M_r(z_i)\|_{\mathsf F} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma), \qquad 1\le i\le s,
nodes.label: eq:Lq-conditional-Mr

nodes.name: Step 3: conditional expansion and the Gaussian term
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 3: Conditional expansion and the Gaussian term.} \medskip In what follows, let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) denote the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(0\le r\le p\) and \(B\in(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}\), write \[ B = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d B_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}, \] and define \[ T[Z^{p-r},B] := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d B_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} T( \underbrace{Z,\ldots,Z}_{p-r\text{ times}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ). \] When \(r=p\), the \(Z\)-arguments are omitted; when $r=0$, $T[Z^p] = T(Z,\ldots,Z)$. Since symmetrizing \(T\) does not change \(T(Z,\ldots,Z)\) and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\) is symmetric. We prove the desired estimate simultaneously for all \(q\ge1\) and all finite-dimensional target Hilbert spaces by induction on \(p\). For \(p=1\), the function \[ x\longmapsto\|T(x)\|_{\mathcal H}^q \] is convex. Hence the assumed convex domination and Proposition~\ref{prop:Hilbert-Gaussian-tensor-Lq} give \[ \|T(Z)\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \|T(G_\Sigma)\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \lesssim \Psi_1(q,\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \] Let \(p\ge2\), and suppose that the assertion has been proved through degree \(p-1\). Expanding \(T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)=T(Z+R,\ldots,Z+R)\) by multilinearity produces, for each \(0\le r\le p\), the \(\binom pr\) terms in which \(r\) arguments equal \(R\) and the remaining \(p-r\) equal \(Z\). Since \(T\) is symmetric, all terms with the same \(r\) coincide, and therefore \[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{r=0}^p \binom pr T[Z^{p-r},R^{\otimes r}]. \] Taking conditional expectation given \(Z\), we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T[Z^{p-r},R^{\otimes r}] \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] = T\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ Z^{p-r}, \mathbb{E}[R^{\otimes r}\mid Z] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right]= T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align*} The term corresponding to \(r=0\) is \(T[Z^p]\), while the term corresponding to \(r=1\) vanishes because $M_1(Z) = \mathbb{E}[R\mid Z] = 0$. Consequently, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] = T[Z^p] + \sum_{r=2}^p \binom pr T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align*} Rearranging this identity, we obtain \begin{align} T[Z^p] = \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] - \sum_{r=2}^p \binom pr T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align} We next control $\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right]$. Since \(y\mapsto\|y\|_{\mathcal H}^q\) is convex for \(q\ge1\), conditional Jensen's inequality gives \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{\mathcal H}^q\le \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ \big\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^q \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right]= \mathbb{E} \big\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^q. \end{align*} Taking \(q\)-th roots and applying Proposition~\ref{prop:Hilbert-Gaussian-tensor-Lq} yield \begin{align} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le g_p \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}, \end{align} where \(g_p\) depends only on \(p\).
nodes.statement_short: Expand T(G,...,G) conditionally on Z and bound the Gaussian term via Jensen and Proposition 2.3.

nodes.name: Contraction notation
nodes.statement: In what follows, let \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) denote the standard basis vectors of \(\mathbb R^d\). For \(0\le r\le p\) and \(B\in(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}\), write \[ B = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d B_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}, \] and define \[ T[Z^{p-r},B] := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d B_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} T( \underbrace{Z,\ldots,Z}_{p-r\text{ times}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ). \] When \(r=p\), the \(Z\)-arguments are omitted; when $r=0$, $T[Z^p] = T(Z,\ldots,Z)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the contraction T[Z^{p-r},B].

nodes.name: Symmetrization and base case
nodes.statement: Since symmetrizing \(T\) does not change \(T(Z,\ldots,Z)\) and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\) is symmetric. We prove the desired estimate simultaneously for all \(q\ge1\) and all finite-dimensional target Hilbert spaces by induction on \(p\). For \(p=1\), the function \[ x\longmapsto\|T(x)\|_{\mathcal H}^q \] is convex. Hence the assumed convex domination and Proposition~\ref{prop:Hilbert-Gaussian-tensor-Lq} give \[ \|T(Z)\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \|T(G_\Sigma)\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \lesssim \Psi_1(q,\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Assume T symmetric; base case p=1 by convexity and Proposition 2.3.

nodes.name: Multilinear expansion
nodes.statement: Let \(p\ge2\), and suppose that the assertion has been proved through degree \(p-1\). Expanding \(T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)=T(Z+R,\ldots,Z+R)\) by multilinearity produces, for each \(0\le r\le p\), the \(\binom pr\) terms in which \(r\) arguments equal \(R\) and the remaining \(p-r\) equal \(Z\). Since \(T\) is symmetric, all terms with the same \(r\) coincide, and therefore \[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{r=0}^p \binom pr T[Z^{p-r},R^{\otimes r}]. \]
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: expand T(Z+R,...,Z+R) by multilinearity.

nodes.name: Conditional expansion
nodes.statement: Taking conditional expectation given \(Z\), we obtain \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T[Z^{p-r},R^{\otimes r}] \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] = T\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ Z^{p-r}, \mathbb{E}[R^{\otimes r}\mid Z] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right]= T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align*} The term corresponding to \(r=0\) is \(T[Z^p]\), while the term corresponding to \(r=1\) vanishes because $M_1(Z) = \mathbb{E}[R\mid Z] = 0$. Consequently, \begin{align*} \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] = T[Z^p] + \sum_{r=2}^p \binom pr T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align*} Rearranging this identity, we obtain \begin{align} T[Z^p] = \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] - \sum_{r=2}^p \binom pr T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)]. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Condition on Z; the r=1 term vanishes, giving (4.4).

nodes.name: Conditional expansion (4.4)
nodes.statement: T[Z^p] = \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] - \sum_{r=2}^p \binom pr T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)].
nodes.label: eq:Lq-conditional-expansion

nodes.name: Gaussian term
nodes.statement: We next control $\mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right]$. Since \(y\mapsto\|y\|_{\mathcal H}^q\) is convex for \(q\ge1\), conditional Jensen's inequality gives \begin{align*} \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{\mathcal H}^q\le \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ \big\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^q \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right]= \mathbb{E} \big\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^q. \end{align*} Taking \(q\)-th roots and applying Proposition~\ref{prop:Hilbert-Gaussian-tensor-Lq} yield \begin{align} \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le g_p \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}, \end{align} where \(g_p\) depends only on \(p\).
nodes.statement_short: Conditional Jensen and Proposition 2.3 bound the Gaussian term.

nodes.name: Conditional Gaussian term bound (4.5)
nodes.statement: \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| \mathbb{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \,\middle|\, Z \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right] \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left\| T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le g_p \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F},
nodes.label: eq:Lq-conditional-Gaussian

nodes.name: Step 4: lower-order terms and completion of the induction
nodes.statement: \textbf{Step 4: Lower-order terms and completion of the induction.} \medskip For \(2\le r\le p-1\), we equip $\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}$ with its natural Hilbert-space structure. More precisely, if \[ U = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} \otimes e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}, \qquad h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\in\mathcal H, \] then \[ \|U\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}^2 := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d \|h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\|_{\mathcal H}^2. \] Define the \((p-r)\)-linear map \[ \mathcal S_rT: (\mathbb R^d)^{p-r} \longrightarrow \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} \] by \begin{align*} (\mathcal S_rT)(x_1,\ldots,x_{p-r}) := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d T(x_1,\ldots,x_{p-r},e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r})\otimes e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}. \end{align*} By the definition of the Frobenius norm of a multilinear map, \begin{align*} \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F}^2 &= \sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_{p-r}=1}^d \big\| (\mathcal S_rT) (e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_{p-r}}) \big\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}^2\\ &= \sum_{\substack{ j_1,\ldots,j_{p-r}=1\\ i_1,\ldots,i_r=1 }}^d \big\| T( e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_{p-r}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^2= \|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2. \end{align*} Therefore, \[ \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F} = \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \] We next relate \(\mathcal S_rT\) to the contraction appearing in \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-expansion}. By definition, \begin{align*} T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\, T( \underbrace{Z,\ldots,Z}_{p-r\text{ times}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ). \end{align*} Hence, by the triangle inequality followed by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, \begin{align*} \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{\mathcal H} &\le \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d \big| (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} \big|\times \big\| T( Z,\ldots,Z, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ) \big\|_{\mathcal H}\\ &\le \bigg( \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}^2 \bigg)^{1/2} \bigg( \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d \big\| T( Z,\ldots,Z, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^2 \bigg)^{1/2}\\ &= \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F} \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}. \end{align*} Thus, pointwise, \[ \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{\mathcal H} \le \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}} \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F}. \] By \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Mr}, \[ \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma) \] almost surely. Therefore, taking \(L_q\)-norms in the preceding pointwise inequality gives \begin{align} \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma) \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{L_q( \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} )}. \end{align} Let \(Q_k\) denote the constant in the induction hypothesis at degree \(k\). More precisely, the induction hypothesis states that, for every finite-dimensional Hilbert space \(\mathcal K\) and every \(k\)-linear map \[ S:(\mathbb R^d)^k\to\mathcal K, \] one has \[ \big\| S(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal K)} \le Q_k \Psi_k(q,\Sigma) \|S\|_{\mathsf F}. \] The space $\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}$ is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and \(\mathcal S_rT\) is an \((p-r)\)-linear map taking values in this space. We may therefore apply the induction hypothesis at degree \(p-r\) to \(\mathcal S_rT\). This gives \begin{align*} \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{L_q( \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} )} \le Q_{p-r} \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F}= Q_{p-r} \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Substituting this estimate into \eqref{eq:Lq-correction-first-bound}, we obtain \begin{align} \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rQ_{p-r} \rho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align} It remains to compare the two covariance scales. We claim that \begin{equation} \rho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \qquad 2\le r\le p-1. \end{equation} Suppose first that \(r\) is even. Then $\rho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2}$, and hence \begin{align*} \rho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-r-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\\ &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma). \end{align*} Now suppose that \(r\) is odd. Then $\rho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(r-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{1/2}$, and \begin{align*} \rho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{j/2}\\ &\le \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{(j+1)/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \end{align*} where the first inequality uses \(q\ge1\). For every index \(j\) in the last sum, \(j+1\equiv p\pmod 2\), so its summand is one of the summands defining \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\). This proves \eqref{eq:rho-Psi-product}. Combining \eqref{eq:Lq-correction-before-scales} and \eqref{eq:rho-Psi-product}, we conclude that \[ \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rQ_{p-r} \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}, \qquad 2\le r\le p-1. \] The term corresponding to \(r=p\) is estimated directly. By \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Mr}, \begin{align*} \big\| T[M_p(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \|T\|_{\mathsf F} \big\| \|M_p(Z)\|_{\mathsf F} \big\|_{L_q}\le U_p\rho_p(\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\le U_p\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Using the representation of \(T[Z^p]\) in \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-expansion}, and combining the preceding estimates with \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Gaussian}, gives \begin{align*} \|T[Z^p]\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \bigg( g_p + U_p + \sum_{r=2}^{p-1} \binom pr U_rQ_{p-r} \bigg) \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Thus the induction closes with $Q_1:=g_1$ and, for \(p\ge2\), \[ Q_p := g_p + U_p + \sum_{r=2}^{p-1} \binom pr U_rQ_{p-r}, \] where the sum is understood to be empty when \(p=2\). In particular, \(Q_p\) depends only on \(p\) and is independent of \(q\), the dimension $d$, \(\Sigma\), the support of \(Z\), and the strict-slack parameter \(\varepsilon\).
nodes.statement_short: Bound each correction via S_rT, the induction hypothesis and the scale comparison; close the induction.

nodes.name: Tensor-product Hilbert space
nodes.statement: For \(2\le r\le p-1\), we equip $\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}$ with its natural Hilbert-space structure. More precisely, if \[ U = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} \otimes e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}, \qquad h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\in\mathcal H, \] then \[ \|U\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}^2 := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d \|h_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\|_{\mathcal H}^2. \]
nodes.statement_short: Equip H tensor (R^d)^{otimes r} with its Hilbert norm.

nodes.name: The map S_rT
nodes.statement: Define the \((p-r)\)-linear map \[ \mathcal S_rT: (\mathbb R^d)^{p-r} \longrightarrow \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} \] by \begin{align*} (\mathcal S_rT)(x_1,\ldots,x_{p-r}) := \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d T(x_1,\ldots,x_{p-r},e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r})\otimes e_{i_1}\otimes\cdots\otimes e_{i_r}. \end{align*} By the definition of the Frobenius norm of a multilinear map, \begin{align*} \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F}^2 &= \sum_{j_1,\ldots,j_{p-r}=1}^d \big\| (\mathcal S_rT) (e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_{p-r}}) \big\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}^2\\ &= \sum_{\substack{ j_1,\ldots,j_{p-r}=1\\ i_1,\ldots,i_r=1 }}^d \big\| T( e_{j_1},\ldots,e_{j_{p-r}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^2= \|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2. \end{align*} Therefore, \[ \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F} = \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Define S_rT and show ||S_rT||_F=||T||_F.

nodes.name: Pointwise Cauchy-Schwarz bound
nodes.statement: We next relate \(\mathcal S_rT\) to the contraction appearing in \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-expansion}. By definition, \begin{align*} T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}\, T( \underbrace{Z,\ldots,Z}_{p-r\text{ times}}, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ). \end{align*} Hence, by the triangle inequality followed by the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality, \begin{align*} \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{\mathcal H} &\le \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d \big| (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r} \big|\times \big\| T( Z,\ldots,Z, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ) \big\|_{\mathcal H}\\ &\le \bigg( \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d (M_r(Z))_{i_1,\ldots,i_r}^2 \bigg)^{1/2} \bigg( \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_r=1}^d \big\| T( Z,\ldots,Z, e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_r} ) \big\|_{\mathcal H}^2 \bigg)^{1/2}\\ &= \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F} \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}}. \end{align*} Thus, pointwise, \[ \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{\mathcal H} \le \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}} \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F}. \] By \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Mr}, \[ \|M_r(Z)\|_{\mathsf F} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma) \] almost surely. Therefore, taking \(L_q\)-norms in the preceding pointwise inequality gives \begin{align} \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma) \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{L_q( \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} )}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Bound the correction pointwise and take L_q norms using (4.3).

nodes.name: Correction term first bound (4.6)
nodes.statement: \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_r\rho_r(\Sigma) \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{L_q( \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} )}.
nodes.label: eq:Lq-correction-first-bound

nodes.name: Apply the induction hypothesis
nodes.statement: Let \(Q_k\) denote the constant in the induction hypothesis at degree \(k\). More precisely, the induction hypothesis states that, for every finite-dimensional Hilbert space \(\mathcal K\) and every \(k\)-linear map \[ S:(\mathbb R^d)^k\to\mathcal K, \] one has \[ \big\| S(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal K)} \le Q_k \Psi_k(q,\Sigma) \|S\|_{\mathsf F}. \] The space $\mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r}$ is a finite-dimensional Hilbert space, and \(\mathcal S_rT\) is an \((p-r)\)-linear map taking values in this space. We may therefore apply the induction hypothesis at degree \(p-r\) to \(\mathcal S_rT\). This gives \begin{align*} \big\| (\mathcal S_rT)(Z,\ldots,Z) \big\|_{L_q( \mathcal H\otimes(\mathbb R^d)^{\otimes r} )} \le Q_{p-r} \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|\mathcal S_rT\|_{\mathsf F}= Q_{p-r} \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Substituting this estimate into \eqref{eq:Lq-correction-first-bound}, we obtain \begin{align} \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rQ_{p-r} \rho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the induction hypothesis at degree p-r to S_rT.

nodes.name: Correction term bound before scale comparison (4.7)
nodes.statement: \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rQ_{p-r} \rho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}.
nodes.label: eq:Lq-correction-before-scales

nodes.name: Scale comparison
nodes.statement: It remains to compare the two covariance scales. We claim that \begin{equation} \rho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \qquad 2\le r\le p-1. \end{equation} Suppose first that \(r\) is even. Then $\rho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2}$, and hence \begin{align*} \rho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-r-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\\ &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma). \end{align*} Now suppose that \(r\) is odd. Then $\rho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(r-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{1/2}$, and \begin{align*} \rho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{j/2}\\ &\le \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{(j+1)/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \end{align*} where the first inequality uses \(q\ge1\). For every index \(j\) in the last sum, \(j+1\equiv p\pmod 2\), so its summand is one of the summands defining \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\). This proves \eqref{eq:rho-Psi-product}.
nodes.statement_short: Prove rho_r Psi_{p-r} <= Psi_p by parity of r.

nodes.name: State the comparison
nodes.statement: It remains to compare the two covariance scales. We claim that \begin{equation} \rho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \qquad 2\le r\le p-1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Claim rho_r(Sigma)Psi_{p-r}(q,Sigma) <= Psi_p(q,Sigma).

nodes.name: Comparison of covariance scales rho_r Psi_{p-r} <= Psi_p (4.8)
nodes.statement: \rho_r(\Sigma) \Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) \le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \qquad 2\le r\le p-1.
nodes.label: eq:rho-Psi-product

nodes.name: Even r
nodes.statement: Suppose first that \(r\) is even. Then $\rho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2}$, and hence \begin{align*} \rho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{r/2} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-r-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\\ &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Even r: the summands match those of Psi_p.

nodes.name: Odd r
nodes.statement: Now suppose that \(r\) is odd. Then $\rho_r(\Sigma) = \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(r-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{1/2}$, and \begin{align*} \rho_r(\Sigma)\Psi_{p-r}(q,\Sigma) &= \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{j/2}\\ &\le \sum_{\substack{ 0\le j\le p-r\\ j\equiv p-r\!\!\!\!\pmod 2 }} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j-1)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{(j+1)/2}q^{(j+1)/2}\le \Psi_p(q,\Sigma), \end{align*} where the first inequality uses \(q\ge1\). For every index \(j\) in the last sum, \(j+1\equiv p\pmod 2\), so its summand is one of the summands defining \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\). This proves \eqref{eq:rho-Psi-product}.
nodes.statement_short: Odd r: use q>=1 to shift each summand to one of Psi_p.

nodes.name: Correction bound
nodes.statement: Combining \eqref{eq:Lq-correction-before-scales} and \eqref{eq:rho-Psi-product}, we conclude that \[ \big\| T[Z^{p-r},M_r(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le U_rQ_{p-r} \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}, \qquad 2\le r\le p-1. \]
nodes.statement_short: Each correction is at most U_r Q_{p-r} Psi_p ||T||_F.

nodes.name: Top-order term
nodes.statement: The term corresponding to \(r=p\) is estimated directly. By \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Mr}, \begin{align*} \big\| T[M_p(Z)] \big\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \|T\|_{\mathsf F} \big\| \|M_p(Z)\|_{\mathsf F} \big\|_{L_q}\le U_p\rho_p(\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\le U_p\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: The r=p term is bounded by U_p rho_p <= U_p Psi_p.

nodes.name: Close the induction
nodes.statement: Using the representation of \(T[Z^p]\) in \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-expansion}, and combining the preceding estimates with \eqref{eq:Lq-conditional-Gaussian}, gives \begin{align*} \|T[Z^p]\|_{L_q(\mathcal H)} \le \bigg( g_p + U_p + \sum_{r=2}^{p-1} \binom pr U_rQ_{p-r} \bigg) \Psi_p(q,\Sigma) \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{align*} Thus the induction closes with $Q_1:=g_1$ and, for \(p\ge2\), \[ Q_p := g_p + U_p + \sum_{r=2}^{p-1} \binom pr U_rQ_{p-r}, \] where the sum is understood to be empty when \(p=2\). In particular, \(Q_p\) depends only on \(p\) and is independent of \(q\), the dimension $d$, \(\Sigma\), the support of \(Z\), and the strict-slack parameter \(\varepsilon\).
nodes.statement_short: Sum the bounds; Q_p depends only on p.

nodes.name: Remove the reduction
nodes.statement: This proves the desired estimate in the finite-support strict-slack case. The approximation argument in \textbf{Step~1} completes the proof in full generality.
nodes.statement_short: Step 1's approximation gives the general case.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement:
By orthogonal invariance, we may assume that \[ \Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d), \qquad G_\Sigma = \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left( \lambda_1^{1/2}\xi_1,\ldots,\lambda_d^{1/2}\xi_d \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight), \] where \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d\) are independent standard Gaussian random variables; indeed, an orthogonal change of coordinates can be absorbed into \(T\) without changing its Frobenius norm. In these coordinates, \(\|\Sigma\|=\max_{1\le i\le d}\lambda_i\) and \(\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i^2\). Since symmetrizing \(T\) does not change \(T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)\) and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\) is symmetric. Writing \(T_{i_1,\ldots,i_p}:=T(e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_p})\in\mathcal H\), we have  egin{align} T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_p=1}^d \lambda_{i_1}^{1/2}\cdots\lambda_{i_p}^{1/2} T_{i_1,\ldots,i_p} \xi_{i_1}\cdots\xi_{i_p}. \end{align} \medskip 
oindent	extbf{Step 1: Chaos decomposition.} \medskip Let \(H_r\) denote the probabilists' Hermite polynomial of degree \(r\). For an ordered \(j\)-tuple \(\mathbf k=(k_1,\ldots,k_j)\in\{1,\ldots,d\}^j\), define \[ 
u_\ell(\mathbf k) :=  igl|\{r:k_r=\ell\} igr|, \qquad H_{\mathbf k}(\xi) := \prod_{\ell=1}^d H_{
u_\ell(\mathbf k)}(\xi_\ell), \] with the convention \(H_{\varnothing}=1\). Since \(\sum_{\ell=1}^d
u_\ell(\mathbf k)=j\), the multivariate Hermite polynomial \(H_{\mathbf k}(\xi)\) has total Hermite degree \(j\) and hence belongs to the \(j\)-th homogeneous Gaussian chaos. When \(j\ge1\), it is also centered. Indeed, at least one of the multiplicities \(
u_\ell(\mathbf k)\) is positive, so independence, together with \(\mathbb{E} H_m(\xi_\ell)=0\) for \(m\ge1\), yields \(\mathbb{E} H_{\mathbf k}(\xi)=0\). For \(0\le a\le\lfloor p/2floor\), let \(\mathcal P_a(p)\) be the collection of all choices of \(a\) disjoint pairs of positions in \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\), and let \(V(\pi)\) denote the set of positions covered by \(\pi\in\mathcal P_a(p)\). The Wick expansion in coordinates reads  egin{align} \xi_{i_1}\cdots\xi_{i_p} = \sum_{a=0}^{\lfloor p/2floor} \sum_{\pi\in\mathcal P_a(p)}  igg( \prod_{\{r,s\}\in\pi} \mathbf 1_{\{i_r=i_s\}}  igg) H_{(i_t)_{t
otin V(\pi)}}(\xi), \end{align} where each pair identifies two coordinate indices, while the remaining \(p-2a\) indices form a Hermite polynomial of total degree \(p-2a\). Fix \(a\) and set \(j:=p-2a\). Substituting \eqref{eq:coordinate-Wick-expansion} into \eqref{eq:Gaussian-coordinate-expansion}, the pairs contract \(T\) against \(a\) copies of \(\Sigma\), which leads us to define \[ B^{(a)}_{k_1,\ldots,k_j} := \sum_{r_1,\ldots,r_a=1}^d \lambda_{r_1}\cdots\lambda_{r_a} T_{r_1,r_1,\ldots,r_a,r_a,k_1,\ldots,k_j}, \] so that \(B^{(0)}_{k_1,\ldots,k_p}=T_{k_1,\ldots,k_p}\). Since \(T\) is symmetric, all pairings in \(\mathcal P_a(p)\) give the same contribution, and \(|\mathcal P_a(p)|=p!/(2^aa!j!)\). Consequently, setting \[ Y_j :=  rac{p!}{2^aa!j!} \sum_{k_1,\ldots,k_j=1}^d \lambda_{k_1}^{1/2}\cdots\lambda_{k_j}^{1/2} B^{(a)}_{k_1,\ldots,k_j} H_{(k_1,\ldots,k_j)}(\xi), \] we obtain the chaos decomposition  egin{equation} T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{\substack{0\le j\le p\j\equiv p\!\!\!\pmod{2}}} Y_j, \end{equation} where each \(Y_j\) is an \(\mathcal H\)-valued random variable in the \(j\)-th Gaussian chaos generated by \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d\). More precisely, for every \(u\in\mathcal H\), the scalar random variable \(\langle Y_j,uangle_{\mathcal H}\) is a linear combination of multivariate Hermite polynomials of total Hermite degree \(j\). \medskip 
oindent	extbf{Step 2: Moments of the chaos components.} \medskip The Cauchy--Schwarz inequality gives  egin{align*} \sum_{k_1,\ldots,k_j=1}^d  ig\|B^{(a)}_{k_1,\ldots,k_j} ig\|_{\mathcal H}^2 &\le  igg( \sum_{r_1,\ldots,r_a=1}^d \lambda_{r_1}^2\cdots\lambda_{r_a}^2  igg) \sum_{k_1,\ldots,k_j=1}^d \sum_{r_1,\ldots,r_a=1}^d  ig\| T_{r_1,r_1,\ldots,r_a,r_a,k_1,\ldots,k_j}  ig\|_{\mathcal H}^2 \ &\le \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{2a}\|T\|_{\mathsf F}^2. \end{align*} The Hermite orthogonality relations read \[ \mathbb{E} \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left[ H_{(k_1,\ldots,k_j)}(\xi) H_{(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_j)}(\xi) \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight] = \sum_{\sigma\in S_j} \prod_{r=1}^j \mathbf{1}_{\{k_r=\ell_{\sigma(r)}\}}, \] where \(S_j\) denotes the set of all permutations of \(\{1,\ldots,j\}\). Since \(B^{(a)}_{k_1,\ldots,k_j}\) is symmetric in \(k_1,\ldots,k_j\), expanding \(\mathbb{E}\|Y_j\|_{\mathcal H}^2\) and applying these relations gives \[ \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left(\mathbb{E}\|Y_j\|_{\mathcal H}^2\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight)^{1/2} =  rac{p!}{2^a a! j!}\sqrt{j!}  igg( \sum_{k_1,\ldots,k_j=1}^d \lambda_{k_1}\cdots\lambda_{k_j}  ig\|B^{(a)}_{k_1,\ldots,k_j} ig\|_{\mathcal H}^2  igg)^{1/2} \lesssim_p \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{a} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2} \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \] Here we used the bound on \(B^{(a)}\) established above and \(\lambda_k\le\|\Sigma\|\). The remaining prefactor is absorbed into the implicit constant since \(a\le p/2\) and \(j\le p\). Now let \(q\ge2\), set \(D:=\dim(\mathcal H)\), and let \(u_1,\ldots,u_D\) be an orthonormal basis of \(\mathcal H\). Each scalar projection \(\langle Y_j,u_rangle_{\mathcal H}\) belongs to the \(j\)-th homogeneous Gaussian chaos. Therefore, Gaussian hypercontractivity \cite[Theorem~5.10]{Janson1997GaussianHilbertSpaces} gives $\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left\| \langle Y_j,u_rangle_{\mathcal H} \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight\|_{L_q} \le (q-1)^{j/2} \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left\| \langle Y_j,u_rangle_{\mathcal H} \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight\|_{L_2}$. Hence, by the triangle inequality in \(L_{q/2}\),  egin{align*} \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left(\mathbb{E}\|Y_j\|_{\mathcal H}^q\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight)^{2/q} &=  igg\| \sum_{r=1}^D ig|\langle Y_j,u_rangle_{\mathcal H} ig|^2  igg\|_{L_{q/2}} \le \sum_{r=1}^D  ig\|\langle Y_j,u_rangle_{\mathcal H} ig\|_{L_q}^2 \le (q-1)^j\,\mathbb{E}\|Y_j\|_{\mathcal H}^2, \end{align*} and combining the two displays with \(a=(p-j)/2\) gives  egin{equation} \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left(\mathbb{E}\|Y_j\|_{\mathcal H}^q\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight)^{1/q} \lesssim_p \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2} \|T\|_{\mathsf F}. \end{equation} \medskip 
oindent	extbf{Step 3: Completion of the proof.} \medskip Applying the triangle inequality to \eqref{eq:Gaussian-coordinate-chaos-decomposition} and using \eqref{eq:Gaussian-coordinate-chaos-Lq}, we obtain \[ \mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\mathopen{}\mathclose group\left(\mathbb{E} ig\|T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) ig\|_{\mathcal H}^q\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroupight)^{1/q} \lesssim_p \sum_{\substack{0\le j\le p\j\equiv p\!\!\!\pmod{2}}} \|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^{(p-j)/2} \|\Sigma\|^{j/2}q^{j/2} \|T\|_{\mathsf F} = \Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\|T\|_{\mathsf F}, \] which is the first estimate for \(q\ge2\). Every \(Y_j\) with \(j\ge1\) is centered, and \(Y_0\), which is present only when \(p\) is even, is deterministic; hence \(Y_0=\mathbb{E} T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)\) and \[ T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) - \mathbb{E} T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{\substack{1\le j\le p\j\equiv p\!\!\!\pmod{2}}} Y_j. \] Repeating the preceding estimate over this restricted range gives the second estimate for \(q\ge2\), with \(\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\) replaced by \(\Psi_p^\circ(q,\Sigma)\). Finally, for \(1\le q<2\) both estimates follow from the case \(q=2\) by monotonicity of \(L_q\)-norms, since \(\Psi_p(2,\Sigma)\le2^{p/2}\Psi_p(q,\Sigma)\) and \(\Psi_p^\circ(2,\Sigma)\le2^{p/2}\Psi_p^\circ(q,\Sigma)\) for \(q\ge1\).
nodes.statement_short: Wick/Hermite chaos decomposition of T(G,...,G), L_2 bounds on each chaos component and hypercontractivity, then the triangle inequality.

nodes.name: Diagonalization and symmetrization
nodes.statement: By orthogonal invariance, we may assume that \[ \Sigma = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d), \qquad G_\Sigma = \mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\mathopen{}\mathclose\bgroup\left( \lambda_1^{1/2}\xi_1,\ldots,\lambda_d^{1/2}\xi_d \aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\aftergroup\egroup\right), \] where \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_d\) are independent standard Gaussian random variables; indeed, an orthogonal change of coordinates can be absorbed into \(T\) without changing its Frobenius norm. In these coordinates, \(\|\Sigma\|=\max_{1\le i\le d}\lambda_i\) and \(\|\Sigma\|_{\mathsf F}^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\lambda_i^2\). Since symmetrizing \(T\) does not change \(T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma)\) and cannot increase \(\|T\|_{\mathsf F}\), we may assume without loss of generality that \(T\) is symmetric. Writing \(T_{i_1,\ldots,i_p}:=T(e_{i_1},\ldots,e_{i_p})\in\mathcal H\), we have \begin{align} T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_p=1}^d \lambda_{i_1}^{1/2}\cdots\lambda_{i_p}^{1/2} T_{i_1,\ldots,i_p} \xi_{i_1}\cdots\xi_{i_p}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Diagonalize Sigma, assume T symmetric and expand in coordinates.

nodes.name: Coordinate expansion of T(G,...,G) (4.9)
nodes.statement: T(G_\Sigma,\ldots,G_\Sigma) = \sum_{i_1,\ldots,i_p=1}^d \lambda_{i_1}^{1/2}\cdots\lambda_{i_p}^{1/2} T_{i_1,\ldots,i_p} \xi_{i_1}\cdots\xi_{i_p}.
nodes.label: eq:Gaussian-coordinate-expansion

nodes.name: Step 1: chaos decomposition
nodes.statement:
extbf{Step 1: Chaos decomposition.} \medskip Let \(H_r\) denote the probabilists' Hermite polynomial of degree \(r\). For an ordered \(j\)-tuple \(\mathbf k=(k_1,\ldots,k_j)\in\{1,\ldots,d\}^j\), define \[ 
u_\ell(\mathbf k) :=  igl|\{r:k_r=\ell\} igr|, \qquad H_{\mathbf k}(\xi) := \prod_{\ell=1}^d H_{
u_\ell(\mathbf k)}(\xi_\ell), \] with the convention \(H_{\varnothing}=1\). Since \(\sum_{\ell=1}^d
u_\ell(\mathbf k)=j\), the multivariate Hermite polynomial \(H_{\mathbf k}(\xi)\) has total Hermite degree \(j\) and hence belongs to the \(j\)-th homogeneous Gaussian chaos. When \(j\ge1\), it is also centered. Indeed, at least one of the multiplicities \(
u_\ell(\mathbf k)\) is positive, so independence, together with \(\mathbb{E} H_m(\xi_\ell)=0\) for \(m\ge1\), yields \(\mathbb{E} H_{\mathbf k}(\xi)=0\). For \(0\le a\le\lfloor p/2floor\), let \(\mathcal P_a(p)\) be the collection of all choices of \(a\) disjoint pairs of positions in \(\{1,\ldots,p\}\), and let \(V(\pi)\) denote the set of positions covered by \(\pi\in\mathcal P_a(p)\). The Wick expansion in coordinates reads  egin{align} \xi_{i_1}\cdots\xi_{i_p} = \sum_{a=0}^{\lfloor p/2floor} \sum_{\pi\in\mathcal P_a(p)}  igg( \prod_{\{r,s\}\in\pi} \mathbf 1_{\{i_r=i_s\}}  igg) H_{(i_t)_{t
otin V(\pi)}}(\xi), \end{align} where each pair identifies two coordinate indices, while the remaining \(p-2a\) indices form a Hermite polynomial of total degree \(p-2a\). Fix \(a\) and set \(j:=p-2a\).
